book-little-ants-big-plan-3: In autumn when the leaves fall down, the ants must keep food underground.
book-little-ants-big-plan-4: The Queen wants food to fill the store, so all the ants must work some more.
book-little-ants-big-plan-5: Little Ant begins to shout about a place he read about. “A restaurant is what we need, a place where people go to feed. It says so in the books I read.”
book-little-ants-big-plan-6: The ants go marching one by one. They march into the setting sun.
book-little-ants-big-plan-7: And Little Ant said “Hey, there’s one!”
book-little-ants-big-plan-8: The ants go marching one by one, carrying a burger, carrying a bun.
book-little-ants-big-plan-9: When they return the Queen is glad. The stores are full. They cheer like mad.
book-little-ants-big-plan-10: Ant gets hugs from mum and dad.
book-little-ants-big-plan-11: His baby sister takes his hand “Now I think I understand.” “The way you love to read a book ... Makes me want to take a look.”
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-0: Lara the ladybird was a special bug. Unlike all her friends, she had bright yellow wings.
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-1: Everyone loved her yellow wings. Each morning, Bibi Butterfly said hello. And Manto Mantis always waved.
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-2: Even Sesa, the sulky spider, was happy to see her. At school, she played with lots of friends.
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-3: But Lara wanted to be like the other ladybirds. “I wish I had red wings like you, Mama,” she cried.
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-4: So one day, to cheer her up, Lara’s mother painted her wings bright red.
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-5: The next morning, nobody greeted Lara on her way to school.
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-6: And when she got there, none of her friends said hello.
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-7: Lara sat all alone. No one noticed her new red wings. Until Miss Miya spotted her and said: “You’ve painted your lovely yellow wings!”
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-8: Lara’s classmates were shocked. “Your wings are special!” “So unique!”“So rare!”
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-9: “Lara,” Miss Miya said, “your yellow wings are what make you you. Like Sipho’s spot ... and Sally’s legs.”
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-10: Back home, Lara took a long bath and scrubbed until her golden wings gleamed. “I’ll never paint my wings again!” she thought. Except, maybe once or twice ...
book-lara-the-yellow-ladybird-11: To try a bit of purple ... or something nice. But not for ever and just for fun.
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-0: It is one week until Thato’s birthday. That’s seven whole days!
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-1: His mama says: “Your birthday present will be a Big surprise!” Thato wonders: what will it be?
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-2: On Monday Thato thinks: Maybe I will get giant wings so I can fly high in the sky like a bird...”
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-3: On Tuesday Thato thinks: “Maybe I will have a birthday cake as big as a house!”
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-4: On Wednesday Thato thinks: “Maybe I will get a rocket ship to whizz up to the moon.
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-5: On Thursday Thato thinks: “Maybe I will get fins so I can swim under the water like a fish.”
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-6: On Friday Thato thinks: “Maybe I will get magic soccer boots and score a thousand goals!”
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-7: On Saturday Thato thinks: “Maybe I will get a key that opens a box filled with treasure!”
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-8: On Sunday it is Thato’s birthday. Mama smiles and says: “Come and see your surprise!”
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-9: It is the best present ever. Thato’s big brother Kudzai has come to visit all the way from the big city!
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-10: Thato smiles and smiles and his big brother lifts him up in the air and hugs him. Kudzai asks:“What do you want to do for your birthday, little brother?”
book-thatos-birthday-surprise-11: And Thato knows exactly what they will do the whole day long.
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-0: Londi was a dreaming girl. Up in the sky, she didn’t see clouds.
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-1: Instead Londi saw flying geese, jumping fish, and fluffy sheep running home.
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-2: One afternoon, Gogo came outside, looking tired. “Londi, stop dreaming!” she said. “It’s time to go and fetch the water.”
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-3: Londi stood up and smiled at her feet. “Let’s go, feet! You know the way there!”
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-4: Londi started walking to the tap. She hopped over the rocks. She crept past Mama Neli’s house. She dashed down the path.
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-5: The line at the tap was long. “Oh no!” Londi said to her feet. “We’ll have to wait. Let’s stay in line. No dreaming away!”
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-6: Ooh! Londi thought. But what’s that shining over there? I wonder who lost their shoe?
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-7: Did it belong to a girl like me? Or something else...
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-8: And what’s that under there? Cheep! Cheep!
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-9: And what’s that big shadow? Uh oh, it’s Gogo! “Londi, your bucket nearly rolled away!” “Sorry, Gogo. I dreamed too far, again.”
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-10: They filled up the bucket together. Londi watched the big sun sink into the hills. “Come let’s go, my dreaming girl,” said Gogo.
book-londi-the-dreaming-girl-11: “Look, Gogo! There’s a pink pig in the sky!” “Oh Londi... It’s just a cloud,” Gogo sighed. Londi took Gogo’s hand and they walked home together happily.
book-walking-together-0: When we go walking and the road is long, we’ll walk together singing a song.
book-walking-together-1: I am with you and you are with me. A journey is fun with our family.
book-walking-together-2: I’ll keep you cosy like a mother hen. She keeps her chicks warm under her wing.
book-walking-together-3: If the rain starts to fall down from the sky, like that good hat I’ll keep your face dry.
book-walking-together-4: If storm clouds get angry and grumble and moan, be brave, why cry? You’re not alone.
book-walking-together-5: We’re walking together so we never get bored. Look up! Look around! See where we’ve explored!
book-walking-together-6: If you see something that’s funny to see, I don’t want to miss it. Please share it with me!
book-walking-together-7: If your feet start to hurt from the distance we’ve passed, don’t worry, we’ve made it! Here’s the clinic at last.
book-walking-together-8: We all need to check our throat, lungs and ears. Get strong as you grow, it’s no reason for tears.
book-walking-together-9: Do you think it’s scary? Here, hold my hand. She’ll check your blood pressure with this clever armband.
book-walking-together-10: They give us our medicine, tell us what we should know, to keep us all healthy. Now back home we go.
book-walking-together-11: It’s okay to be tired, there’s so much we’ve seen. Now it’s your bedtime. Sleep well and sweet dreams.
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-0: Nita’s hanging upside down, her long hair tickling at the ground. The trees, the grass, the everything is all the wrong way round.
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-1: Her feet, they poke into the sky. Little Navi’s walking by. He says ‘I’ve seen you here before. You’re upside down again! What for?’
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-2: His feet swim lightly in the air. She tries to hide behind her hair. ‘It’s h-h-h-hard to t-t-talk’, she says to him. ‘I’m not the same. I don’t fit in.
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-3: Navi takes her by the hand. He wants to help her understand. They climb to Navi’s look-out spot. From up here they can see a lot. They perch and have a quiet stare at children playing here and there.
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-5: Those kids are not the same at all. Abe’s round. Chi's freckled.
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-7: Bambam’s wild and must be free, while Lulu's reading quietly.
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-10: And me, I am just skin and bone. And you are you. You’re not alone. Each human’s sort of strange, you see. That makes you just the same, like me. This world is really one big game. To play, we can’t all be the same.
book-why-is-nita-upside-down-11: Nita feels the right way round, thanks to the new friend she's found. Upside down was never fun. Now she plays with everyone.
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-0: One day, Mr Sloth came to visit. He said: I’m sleepy! I need a good branch for a bed!
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-1: I’m quite good at climbing. I know how to swing. But sleeping’s my favourite, favourite thing!
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-2: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here. And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-3: Oh no, Mr Sloth! A giraffe’s eating there! He might think you’re lunch and start nibbling your hair!
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-4: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here. And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-5: Oh no, Mr Sloth! There’s a beehive right there! You’ll never get sleep with those bees everywhere!
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-6: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here. And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-7: Oh no, Mr Sloth, that’s a snake over there! Not a branch! Poor old snake. You gave him quite a scare.
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-8: This branch looks lovely! I think I’ll sleep here. And you? Don’t you think that’s a splendid idea?
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-9: Oh no, Mr Sloth! There’s a bird squawking there! You’ll never get sleep with that noise in the air!
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-10: Try climb one more branch, Mr Sloth! they all said. And that branch was just the right one for his bed.
book-sleepy-mr-sloth-11: The bird and the snake, the giraffe and each bee were happy to have Mr Sloth in their tree.
book-lory-dory-0: One night Grandpa was tucking me in. His hands were soft and his hair was thin.
book-lory-dory-1: ‘I’m going to tell you a special story, about a girl named Lory Dory.’
book-lory-dory-2: You couldn’t see Lory Dory at all because she was born invisible.
book-lory-dory-3: You’d only see Lory when rain hit her head, or when she was curled under blankets in bed.
book-lory-dory-4: Lory was left out of all the kids’ games. They teased her and they called her names. ‘Look, it’s Lory. The Imaginary Friend! She’s not like us, she’s just pretend!’
book-lory-dory-5: One day at school, a boy wanted to know: ‘How do you look? I only see you in snow.’
book-lory-dory-6: ‘Can you paint yourself?’ Lory knew that she could. But not in the same way the boy thought she would.
book-lory-dory-7: Lory painted her body with all that she loved from the world all around and the sky up above.
book-lory-dory-8: She painted herself every day with such pride, to bring out the person who she was inside.
book-lory-dory-9: I know I’m invisible and hard to see. So I painted these pictures to show the real me.’
book-lory-dory-10: ‘Are you making this up, Gramps? Is this story true?’ ‘Lory is real – real as me, real as you.’
book-lory-dory-11: When Grandpa had left me, I can’t quite be sure, but I think I saw Lory just outside my door.
book-sima-and-siza-0: Simamkele loves dolls. Mama buys him lots. They keep his loneliness away. Sima’s favourite doll is Siza. Sima wants to be a nurse when he grows up.
book-sima-and-siza-1: He loves to put on Mama’s skirt, and twirl. Like magic, he suddenly becomes Sima the nurse. He plays hospital-hospital and makes sickly Siza and all his dolls better.
book-sima-and-siza-2: Wherever Sima is, Siza is there too.
book-sima-and-siza-3: But Sima’s friends do not like Siza. One day, they took him away and stuck his head in the toilet.
book-sima-and-siza-4: When Papa came home, Sima was nursing Siza. ‘What are you doing?’ asked Papa. ‘I’m being a nurse,’ said Sima. ‘Will you play with me?’ ‘Yes. But we will go to the park and play soccer,’ said Papa.
book-sima-and-siza-5: His friends saw Sima and Papa playing soccer. They joined in. Sima and Papa often play soccer now. But they still haven’t played with dolls.
book-sima-and-siza-6: One day, Sima was playing hospital-hospital with his dolls. He heard Mama shout. ‘Sima! Run! Papa is waiting to play with you at the park.’
book-sima-and-siza-7: ‘Why on earth are you wearing a dress?’ said Papa in an angry voice. Just then a ball flew out of nowhere and ...
book-sima-and-siza-8: ... knocked Papa down. Everyone panicked. Except Sima. He knelt and tied his blanket around Papa’s bleeding head. ‘Call an ambulance!’ he shouted.
book-sima-and-siza-9: ‘He needs stitches in his head. You did just the right thing,’ said the nurse. Sima was proud.
book-sima-and-siza-10: ‘You’re a hero. You’ll make a great doctor one day.’ ‘But I want to be a nurse, just like you,’ said Sima.
book-sima-and-siza-11: ‘Thank you, Nurse Sima,’ said Papa. Now Sima and Papa play hospital-hospital and soccer – and his friends do too.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-0: Nestled in the Kingdom of the Zulu is a magnificent place called the Valley.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-1: A little girl called Jabulile lives here. Jabulile was always a happy child. She was also curious, and full of questions about life. Everything fascinated her.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-2: Jabulile’s father was a mielie farmer. Her mother was a teacher. They taught her to dream big dreams. Jabulile’s biggest dream was to help people.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-3: Everyone in the village was Jabulile’s friend, especially the elders. They taught her about the wise men and women who once lived in the Valley. Jabulile also wanted to be wise.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-4: One awful day, the clouds began to gather over the Valley. Everything grew dark and grey. An ugly storm swept over the land.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-5: Great gusts of wind blew the roofs off the huts. All the animals lost their homes. It was a very sad day.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-6: The village folk cried, “What shall we do now?” “All the crops are ruined!” cried the farmers. “Our homes are gone!” said the elders. All hope seemed lost. But Jabulile remembered something her wise father once told her.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-7: Jabulile started speaking to the villagers. “The storm only hurts us,” she said, “because of the way we choose to see it. If you look up the sun is shining again. It is a new day. “After every storm, there must be a rainbow!” she shouted excitedly.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-8: Just then a glorious rainbow appeared in the sky.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-9: The villagers saw the rainbow and they began to smile. It stood as a promise that the storm was over.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-10: The villagers rebuilt their homes. Farmers planted new crops. The grass grew greener than ever before.
book-there-must-be-a-rainbow-11: Once again there was hope and happiness in the Valley.
book-amazing-daisy-0: Once upon a time on a little farm near a little village there lived a little chicken called Daisy.
book-amazing-daisy-1: “When I grow up, I want to fly high, high into the sky,” Daisy said. But all the other chickens laughed at her.
book-amazing-daisy-2: “You are so weird,” they said. “We won’t play with you anymore.” “Daisy, we can all flap our wings but it’s very difficult for chickens to fly,” Mama told her.
book-amazing-daisy-3: Daisy wouldn’t give up. Every day she practised by herself, flapping her wings. Flap, flap, flap, she would flap her wings but she couldn’t lift off the ground.
book-amazing-daisy-4: While she practised, she imagined herself flying high into the sky and looking at the chickens below. She imagined herself flying past the sparrows and past the swallows. “Wow!” the birds would say. “A chicken that can fly!”
book-amazing-daisy-5: So ... Flap, flap, flap, every day Daisy would flap her wings. She would lift off the ground but fall down again.
book-amazing-daisy-6: “I’m never going to fly!” Daisy cried to Mama. “The others are right.” “Daisy, you are different from the other chickens. They don’t want to fly but you do! You can do it,” Mama said.
book-amazing-daisy-7: The following day Daisy climbed to the top of the chicken coop and flap, flap, flap, she flapped her wings. She flew into the air and flapped her wings ... and flapped her wings ... and flapped her wings and ...
book-amazing-daisy-8: Bam! The other chickens laughed out loud.“Ha ha ha! We told you! Chickens can’t fly!”
book-amazing-daisy-9: But the next day Daisy climbed even higher, right up to the top of the rondavel. Flap, flap, flap, Daisy flapped her wings. She flew into the air and flapped her wings ... and flapped her wings ... and flapped her wings and ...
book-amazing-daisy-10: She kept flying! The wind beneath her wings grew stronger and she flew higher and higher! The sparrows and the swallows said, “Amazing! A flying chicken!”
book-amazing-daisy-11: And the other chickens wanted to be just like her. They said, “Oh Daisy, you’re amazing!”
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-0: One day Tortoise was walking through the veld. He was searching and searching. He gazed into the distance and squinted at the grass. “Are you looking for something?” Snail asked. “Yes, I’m looking for my house. Have you seen it?”
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-1: “No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!” She climbed onto Tortoise’s shell. Tortoise walked on with Snail on his back. They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house.
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-2: “Are you looking for something?” asked Sparrow. “Yes, we're looking for Tortoise's house. Have you seen it?” “No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!”
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-3: Sparrow flapped his wings and he whizzed away. “You’re going too fast!” called Tortoise. “Alright, then I’ll hop on too.” Tortoise walked on with Snail and Sparrow perched on his shell. They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house.
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-4: “Are you looking for something?” asked Ladybird. “Yes, we’re looking for Tortoise’s house. Have you seen it?”
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-5: “No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!” Ladybird hopped onto Tortoise’s shell. Tortoise walked on with Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird sitting on his back. They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house. A breeze started to blow.
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-6: “Are you looking for something?” asked Mouse. “Yes, Mouse, I’m looking for my house. Have you seen it?” “No, I haven’t, but I’ll help you look!”
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-7: Mouse jumped onto Tortoise’s back. Tortoise walked on with Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird and Mouse on his back. They looked and looked, but there was no sign of a house. The wind swept the leaves off the ground and swirled them around Tortoise.
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-8: The wind got stronger and stronger. The sky turned dark. “Oh, where is my house?” Tortoise sighed. Thunder roared in the hills. Lightning flashed in the distance. Drip, drip came the rain. “Oh, where is Tortoise’s house?” asked Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird and Mouse.
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-9: The wind whirled and whipped and blew Snail and Sparrow and Ladybird and Mouse right off Tortoise’s back.
book-tortoise-finds-his-home-10: “Eek!” squeaked Tortoise with a fright, and he shrank back into his shell. It was warm and cosy inside. “Oh, here is my house!”
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-0: One day a very clever baby was born in Gungululu in the Eastern Cape. Her name was Sindiwe Magona. She was the oldest of eight children.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-1: At night, her grandmother told magical stories about ogres and giants, animals of the forests, great beasts, and little creatures of the veld. It was Sindiwe’s favourite time.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-2: Sindiwe loved school and she dreamed about being a teacher.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-3: When Sindiwe became a teenager, her family organised a feast to celebrate. She was given special things to wear and a wise old man sang a praise song to her. (Blessings, long life! May your ancestors guard you!)
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-4: Sindiwe trained to be a teacher. She was very excited to teach at her first school. But there weren’t enough schools for black children and they had no desks or books to write in. This made Sindiwe feel scared. How could she be a good teacher when the children had nowhere to sit?
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-5: She left the school to work as a cleaner. She worked in four different houses. Sometimes the people there treated her badly and Sindiwe became very unhappy.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-6: All this time Sindiwe studied. Her hard work paid off! She won a scholarship to study at a university in New York. She and her three small children packed their bags and flew across the sea to the United States of America.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-7: In New York, Sindiwe studied to become a social worker. She wanted to help families make their lives better.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-8: When she finished studying, the United Nations gave Sindiwe a job. Most of the countries in the world meet at the United Nations to talk about their problems.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-9: Sindiwe told the world about South Africa, and how hard it was for black people living there. The people at the United Nations loved to listen to Sindiwe’s stories. They wanted to learn more and more about South Africans. Perhaps, together, they could help to change things in South Africa.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-10: She worked at the United Nations for twenty years while her children grew into adults. But Sindiwe missed the country where she was born. She wanted to tell her stories to the people at home. So she packed her luggage, got on a plane and flew back over the sea to Cape Town.
book-sindiwe-and-the-fireflies-11: Sindiwe’s love for books and stories have helped her write piles and piles of books. And children and grown-ups love to read her stories. Many people call her Nomabali because she’s always writing, telling and reading stories.
book-a-tiny-seed-0: In a village on the slopes of Mount Kenya in East Africa, a little girl worked in the fields with her mother. Her name was Wangari.
book-a-tiny-seed-1: Wangari loved being outside. In her family’s food garden she broke up the soil with her machete. She pressed tiny seeds into the warm earth.
book-a-tiny-seed-2: Her favourite time of day was just after sunset. When it got too dark to see the plants, Wangari knew it was time to go home. She would follow the narrow paths through the fields, crossing rivers as she went.
book-a-tiny-seed-3: Wangari was a clever child and couldn’t wait to go to school. But her mother and father wanted her to stay and help them at home. When she was seven years old, her big brother persuaded her parents to let her go to school.
book-a-tiny-seed-4: She liked to learn! Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read. She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America. Wangari was excited! She wanted to know more about the world.
book-a-tiny-seed-5: At the American university Wangari learnt many new things. She studied plants and how they grow. And she remembered how she grew: playing games with her brothers in the shade of the trees in the beautiful Kenyan forests.
book-a-tiny-seed-6: The more she learnt, the more she realised that she loved the people of Kenya. She wanted them to be happy and free. The more she learnt, the more she remembered her African home.
book-a-tiny-seed-7: When she had finished her studies, she returned to Kenya. But her country had changed. Huge farms stretched across the land. Women had no wood to make cooking fires. The people were poor and the children were hungry.
book-a-tiny-seed-8: Wangari knew what to do. She taught the women how to plant trees from seeds. The women sold the trees and used the money to look after their families. The women were very happy. Wangari had helped them to feel powerful and strong.
book-a-tiny-seed-9: As time passed, the new trees grew into forests, and the rivers started flowing again. Wangari’s message spread across Africa. Today, millions of trees have grown from Wangari’s seeds.
book-a-tiny-seed-10: Wangari had worked hard. People all over the world took notice, and gave her a famous prize. It is called the Nobel Peace Prize, and she was the first African woman ever to receive it.
book-a-tiny-seed-11: Wangari died in 2011, but we can think of her every time we see a beautiful tree.
book-a-dancers-tale-0: Once upon a time, not so far away, a baby called Phyllis was born for ballet. Two people in love, her Mom and her Dad, could not have known yet what a dancer they had.
book-a-dancers-tale-1: When Phyllis was four she had us transfixed: impressing her teachers with ducky feet flicks. Before school and after, she danced every day. Nothing pleased Phyllis more than ballet.
book-a-dancers-tale-2: The world would soon see, when, only fifteen, she travelled to London to live out her dream. Far from home and her friends, she was starting afresh. The Royal Ballet school would soon be impressed!
book-a-dancers-tale-3: When she danced Swan Lake it was fit for the Queen! After years pirouetting, it was time to be seen! She took to the stage, leaping, twirling about, with everyone smiling! They clap and they shout!
book-a-dancers-tale-4: From Mexico to Canada, the US to France, everyone asked her to visit and dance. With the Royal Ballet, and all of her friends, she spread love for dancing so it never would end.
book-a-dancers-tale-5: Still, Phyllis missed home, they’d been too long apart. She longed to return and to make a fresh start. So she leaped and she bounded to her beautiful land, to walk once again on South African sand.
book-a-dancers-tale-6: Dance isn’t just fun, as Phyllis well knew: she worked day and night, and with hard work she grew. Always smiling and tireless, through good times and tough,she aimed for her best.‘Good’ was never enough.
book-a-dancers-tale-7: Romeo and Juliet, Swan Lake and Giselle. She captured each audience under her spell. With Gary Burne beside her, Eduard Greyling too, her dancing was magic in every review.
book-a-dancers-tale-8: Reward comes eventually, when you’re put to the test. And one day South Africa would call her the best: ‘Prima Ballerina Assoluta’, greatest dancer of all, her title forever. Phyllis wanted no more.
book-a-dancers-tale-9: Soon Phyllis found love when she met Philip Boyd, a dancer himself! They were both overjoyed. In love, they soon married, and together they’d dance. No match could be better when given the chance!
book-a-dancers-tale-10: They didn’t have children but never were sad, for they had a way to help all moms and dads. Their school, Dance For All, would give children a chance, from all walks of life, to learn and love dance.
book-a-dancers-tale-11: Her gift to the world and all her success help others to realise they can be their best. They dance for us now, inspired by her feats,inspiring us, too, as we dream in our seats.
